title: Ops economics: self-hosted vs managed inference decision playbook
content:
Executive summary:

This brief synthesizes the operational economics, buyer signals, and competitive positioning we should use when engaging buyers who are evaluating self-hosted inference stacks (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM and similar) versus a managed inference platform (Redwood). The goal is an actionable playbook sales and SEs can use to: 1) qualify build-vs-buy leads faster, 2) surface predictable cost and risk comparisons, and 3) present Redwood’s differentiated value in a way that maps to buyer priorities (latency, cost predictability, compliance, and engineering velocity).

Context and why this matters:
- Many engineering-first buyers are tempted by open-source stacks because of perceived cost savings and control. However, the total cost and operational burden — especially as models, traffic patterns, and quantization strategies change — frequently pushes teams to prefer a managed option.
- Competing stacks: vLLM (fast batching, memory optimizations), TGI (Flexibility, community integrations), TensorRT-LLM (high throughput on NVIDIA with FP16/INT8). All are viable, but each exposes different ops trade-offs that buyers often underestimate.

Decision criteria (what buyers actually care about):
- Latency tail behavior (p95/p99) and predictability
- Unit cost ($/k tokens or $/inference) at target QPS
- Engineering effort and time-to-first-prod (weeks vs months)
- Ongoing ops headcount and on-call risk
- Model agility (how fast to roll a new model or quantization profile)
- Observability and incident response (token-level tracing, per-model dashboards)
- Compliance and data residency requirements

Quick comparative readout (one-paragraph each):
- vLLM: Great for teams that can tolerate iterative tuning — strong memory and batching primitives reduce GPU requirements for many workloads. Requires deep kernel and scheduler tuning for latency-sensitive apps; KV caching and long-context efficiency vary by workload.
- TGI (Text Generation Inference): Fast to integrate, strong for experimenting with multiple model families and plugins. Less optimized for sustained production throughput at low latency without custom infra and engineering investments.
- TensorRT-LLM: Best throughput on NVIDIA hardware when models are fully supported and quantized. High performance but brittle: conversion and quantization steps can be time-consuming and may degrade quality without careful evals.
- Managed (Redwood): Lower time-to-value, predictable SLAs, built-in routing/fallbacks, and cost controls (batching, cache suggestions). Managed does not always minimize raw compute spend for every theoretical workload, but eliminates ops unpredictability and reduces total TCO for most teams.

Operational risk matrix (how to use with buyers):
- Risk axis A: Engineering surface area (low to high) — self-hosted typically high.
- Risk axis B: Uncertainty of unit economics (known vs unknown) — self-hosted often unknown until scale.
- Recommend a simple qualifier question set for AE/SEs to place buyers in the matrix:
  * Do you have 2+ engineers dedicated to inference infra?
  * Do you need <50ms p95 for interactive LLM responses?
  * Will you need audited logs + customer-managed KMS?
  * Are you planning model churn (monthly model swaps / continuous A/B)?
  * Is on-prem or VPC-only required?

Cost comparison framework (example assumptions buyers understand):
- Example buyer profile: 100 qps average, 300 tokens per request, 24/7 usage.
- Self-hosted TCO components: GPU spot/on-demand costs, node overhead (CPU, storage), autoscaler complexity, dev time to optimize batching and quantization, on-call paged incidents.
- Managed TCO components: per-token/embedding price, optional reserved capacity commitment, support/SLA add-on, integration work (usually <2 weeks).
- Quick back-of-envelope: for many customers in our target cohort, the break-even horizon for building in-house is 9–18 months when factoring in SE salaries, on-call, and lost developer productivity for model iteration. Specifics vary dramatically by QPS and model size.

Technical objections and rebuttals (SE-friendly language):
- Objection: 'We can save 40–60% on raw GPU spend by self-hosting.'
  Rebuttal: 'Raw GPU delta is only one piece. We should model the full stack: lost engineering hours for runtime tuning, risk cost from downtime, and slower model iteration. Redwood provides batching/cache profiles and quantization recommendations that capture most of those savings without adding ops cost.'
- Objection: 'We need complete data control; we can’t trust a managed provider.'
  Rebuttal: 'Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) provides customer-managed control plane options, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logs — the same API and rollout tooling you get in hosted mode. We can map the exact security controls to your compliance checklist.'
- Objection: 'TensorRT yields the best latency; managed will never reach that.'
  Rebuttal: 'For narrow, fully-converted models on NVIDIA, TensorRT can win on raw numbers. But conversion cycles, model support, and regression risk are significant. We recommend a hybrid approach: TensorRT for a small set of hottest endpoints, Redwood routing/fallback for general traffic and safety nets.'

Positioning hooks by buyer persona:
- AI platform / infra lead: Emphasize predictable concurrency, autoscaling policies, and the reduction of on-call incidents. Provide the TCO model and a roadmap for reserved capacity commitments.
- Product/ML engineer: Emphasize quick model swaps, canary rollouts, and integrated evals (prevent regressions). Offer a trial integration with existing CI to show <2 week end-to-end.
- Security/compliance: Emphasize Private deployment, KMS, audit logs, and contractual SLAs. Map to SOC2/ISO/PCI controls as needed.

Sales play templates (short scripts):
- Discovery: 'Tell me about the last time model performance or infra surprise caused production impact. How often do you change models in prod?'
- Value pitch for dev-first buyers: 'Most teams that try to build an inference stack spend the first 6 months on low-level tuning — batching, kv cache, quantization — and end up with unpredictable costs. Redwood abstracts that away and gives you the same API and rollout controls across hosted/dedicated/private.'
- Closing/commitment ask: 'We can run a 30-day proof-of-value on a constrained route: we’ll instrument the same traffic to measure latency, cost per token, and error rates; we then recommend a reserved capacity profile if the results are favorable.'

Marketing and collateral suggestions:
- Short one-pager: 'When to build: a flowchart for infra vs managed' (for AE enablement).
- Calculator: simple spreadsheet where a buyer plugs QPS, avg tokens, desired p95, and gets a Redwood vs self-hosted TCO range.
- Engineering blog post: 'Hidden costs of self-hosted inference — our empirical 12-month study' (backed by anonymized customer data).

Competitive nuances to call out in objections library:
- Some OSS projects will tout single-GPU throughput numbers; call that out as synthetic — explain warm-up, knitting quantization, and conversion complexity.
- Multi-model and multi-tenant inference: the ops complexity increases superlinearly; highlight Redwood’s routing/fallback and per-route costing to control this.

Recommended next steps for GTM teams:
1) Create a short AE/SE qualifying checklist based on the decision criteria above (owner: Marco Ruiz).
2) Build the TCO calculator prototype and embed into AE playbooks (owner: Emily Wong).
3) Run two 30-day POVs with customers who sign an NDA: one for a high-QPS interactive app, one for an on-prem regulated app to capture concrete cost and security comparisons (owner: Ben Carter).
4) Produce collateral: one-pager, blog, and a small eval pipeline example repo that automates vLLM/TGI/TensorRT baseline runs (owner: marketing + applied-ml).

Open questions / unknowns to research:
- Empirical p99 comparisons across vLLM, TGI, and TensorRT for 8k and 32k context lengths with representative traffic distributions.
- Real-world ops headcount for customers who attempted self-hosted for >12 months: churn, average on-call pages per month.
- Pricing experiments for Reserved Capacity vs pure usage that close the TCO gap for larger customers more quickly.

Appendix (quick checklist for SE prep before customer call):
- Run short benchmark with customer model (if allowed): measure cold/hot latency and throughput, and collect token distribution.
- Prepare a tailored cost comparison using the TCO framework.
- If buyer requests, map Redwood Private controls to their compliance checklist (bring SOC2/ISO artifacts).

Endnotes:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic and sales-facing. The goal is to accelerate qualification and make cost/risk trade-offs explicit. Keep it living — update after each POV.
summary: Actionable GTM playbook for qualifying build-vs-buy inference decisions; includes buyer decision criteria, cost framework, objection rebuttals, persona hooks, and tactical next steps.
notes: Do not publish externally yet — draft. Use internal links and the TCO calculator prototype when available. Update with POV data after two customer trials.
